mcqs.question: What does the single-machine-vs-distributed check compare the estimate against?
options: The company's total headcount and engineering budget
A single high-end machine's known capacity — RAM, cores, disk IOPS
The peak-to-average traffic ratio used in the original QPS estimate
The number of competing products already running distributed systems
mcqs.explanation: The check compares the workload's numbers directly against a real single machine's capacity envelope. Headcount, competitor architecture, and the peak-to-average ratio are unrelated to whether one machine can handle this specific workload.

mcqs.question: Why can a single machine be unacceptable even when it has plenty of capacity headroom to spare?
options: Machines with spare capacity always run hotter and fail more often than fully-utilized ones
Capacity headroom on a single machine legally requires provisioning a second machine in most jurisdictions
Spare capacity on one machine means the workload is actually smaller than estimated, requiring re-estimation
It's still a single point of failure — one disk or power failure takes the entire service down regardless of remaining capacity
mcqs.explanation: Durability is a separate concern from raw capacity — a single box is still one point of failure no matter how much headroom it has. There's no such reliability or legal rule, and spare capacity doesn't imply a sizing error.

mcqs.question: A workload's real single-machine QPS ceiling depends most on which factor?
options: Whether the workload is CPU-bound, memory-bound, or I/O-bound
The total dollar cost of the machine being considered
Whether the machine is hosted by a major cloud provider or run on-premises
The number of software engineers currently maintaining the service
mcqs.explanation: The resource the workload actually exhausts first — CPU, memory, or I/O — sets the real ceiling, and that ceiling can differ by an order of magnitude between categories. Cost, hosting location, and team size don't determine a machine's throughput ceiling.

mcqs.question: What determines whether a single machine's simplicity or a distributed setup's survivability is the right call, more than raw QPS or data-size numbers alone?
options: The programming language the service happens to be implemented in
Whether the interviewer personally prefers distributed systems as a design style
Whether the system is required to survive a single node failure
Whether the company is a startup or a large, established enterprise
mcqs.explanation: The deciding factor is an explicit durability requirement, not company size, language choice, or interviewer preference — capacity numbers alone don't settle this trade-off.

mcqs.question: Why is defaulting to a distributed, sharded architecture "because that's what interviews want" a weaker answer than checking single-machine capacity first?
options: Distributed architectures are always strictly slower than single-machine designs at any scale
It skips the actual estimation being tested and leaves no numeric justification if asked 'why not just one machine?'
Interviewers penalize any mention of distributed systems in an estimation-focused question
Single machines are always cheaper than distributed systems regardless of the numbers involved
mcqs.explanation: The weakness is having no numbers to back the choice when challenged — the estimation itself was skipped. Distributed systems aren't universally slower or costlier, and interviewers don't blanket-penalize mentioning them, only an unjustified default to them.
